title: Trees in cities, and the ones that die

turns.speaker: Jay
turns.text: They planted four hundred street trees two summers ago and about a third of them are dead.

turns.speaker: Ewan
turns.text: A third is about standard for urban planting, unfortunately. The planting gets funded and the watering doesn't.

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: Which is backwards, because a street tree needs about three years of attention and then nothing for a century.

turns.speaker: Jay
turns.text: So a small maintenance budget would save most of them.

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: A tiny one. But planting has a photograph and watering doesn't.

turns.speaker: Ewan
turns.text: The species choice matters as much, honestly. Half of these are ornamental things that look good on a plan and hate compacted soil.

turns.speaker: Jay
turns.text: What are they actually for? Because the arguments keep changing.

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: The cooling is the serious one. A shaded street can run several degrees below an unshaded one on a hot day, and that's a life-and-death difference for elderly residents.

turns.speaker: Ewan
turns.text: Air quality gets overstated, mind you. Trees intercept some particulates and they can also trap them under a canopy on a narrow street.

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: That's true, and the honest version is cooling first, water management second, air quality a distant third.

turns.speaker: Jay
turns.text: Plus people simply prefer them, which nobody counts.

turns.speaker: Ewan
turns.text: It does show up in property prices, which is the only way anyone measures preference.

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: And is also why the leafy streets are the expensive ones already.

points: About a third of four hundred newly planted street trees died, which is typical because planting is funded and watering is not.
Marisol notes street trees need roughly three years of care and then none for a century.
Species choice matters, as ornamental varieties often cope badly with compacted urban soil.
The strongest benefit is cooling, with shaded streets several degrees cooler, which matters for elderly residents.
Ewan argues air quality benefits are overstated and canopies can trap particulates in narrow streets.
Preference shows up only in property prices, which is also why leafy streets are already expensive.
